title: Remark
body_md:
In the case $k = 3$, Wooley \cite{Woo2015} gives a suitable mean value estimate below exponent 10, using work of Br\"udern and Robert \cite{BR2015}, so one might expect ten variables to suffice for us here. However, the corresponding restriction estimate is not known below this exponent \cite{HW2022}.
For this reason, we have not been able to handle the case $s = 10$ when $k = 3$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Suppose $(a_1,\ldots,a_s) = (b_1,\ldots,b_s)$ and $a_1, \ldots, a_{s-1} > 0$, so that 
\[
a_s = - (a_1 + \cdots + a_{s-1}) < 0.
\]
Writing $p_i  = -a_i/a_s$ $(1 \leqslant i \leqslant s-1)$, we obtain
\[
p_1 x_1^3 + \cdots + p_{s-1} x_{s-1}^3 = (p_1 x_1 + \cdots + p_{s-1} x_{s-1})^3.
\]
This is the equality case of Jensen's inequality, and can only occur if $\mathbf x$ lies on the diagonal. Then $\mathbf x$ is singular. We conclude that $\mathcal V$ contains no non-singular real solutions. As $\mathcal V(\mathbb R)$ is the diagonal in this case, we cannot hope for a density result here anyway.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ARLgen}
Let $J \in \mathbb N$, let ${\varepsilon}, {\delta} > 0$, and let $\mathcal F: \mathbb N \to [1,\infty)$.
For $j \in [J]$, let $\Psi_j(x) \in \mathbb Z[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $k_j$. Let $\mathcal A \subseteq [N]$ with $\# \mathcal A \geqslant {\delta} N$. Then there exist
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item positive integers $M \ll_{{\varepsilon}, {\delta}, \mathcal F, \boldsymbol \Psi} 1$ and $d \leqslant M/J$,
\item for $j \in [J]$, a $(\mathcal F(M), N^{k_j})$-irrational frequency ${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb T^{c_j}$ with \mbox{$c_j \leqslant d$,}
\item an arithmetic progression $\mathcal P \subseteq [N]$ with $\# \mathcal P \geqslant N/M$,
\item and decompositions
\[
1_{\mathcal A} = f + f_{\mathrm{unf}},
\qquad
f 1_{\mathcal P} = f_{\mathrm{str}} + f_{\mathrm{sml}},
\]
\end{enumerate}
such that
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $f: [N] \to [0,1]$,
\item $f_{\mathrm{unf}}: [N] \to [-1,1]$ with
$
\| f_{\mathrm{unf}} \|_{\Phi} \leqslant N / \mathcal F(M),
$
where $\Phi = \mathbb T\textnormal{-span}(\boldsymbol \Psi)$,
\item $f_{\mathrm{sml}}: \mathcal P \to [-2, 2]$ with $\| f_{\mathrm{sml}} \|_2 \leqslant {\varepsilon} \| 1_{\mathcal P} \|_2$,
\item $f_{{\mathrm{str}}}: \mathcal P \to [0,1]$ with $\| f_{\mathrm{str}} \|_1 \gg {\delta} \| 1_{\mathcal P} \|_1$,
\item as well as a trigonometric polynomial 
\[
F: \mathbb T^{c_1} \times \cdots \times \mathbb T^{c_J} \to [0,1]
\]
of degree at most $M$ such that
\[
f_{\mathrm{str}}(n) = F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} \Psi_1(n), \ldots, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(J)} \Psi_J(n))
\qquad (n \in \mathcal P).
\]
\end{enumerate}

label: ARL
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ARL}
Let $k \in \mathbb N$, let ${\varepsilon}, {\delta} > 0$, and let $\mathcal F: \mathbb N \to [1,\infty)$. Let $\mathcal A \subseteq [N]$ with $\# \mathcal A \geqslant {\delta} N$. Then there exist
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item positive integers $M \ll_{{\varepsilon}, {\delta}, \mathcal F} 1$ and $d \leqslant M/2$,
\item for $j \in 
\{ 1, k \}$, a $(\mathcal F(M), N^j)$-irrational frequency ${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb T^{c_j}$ with $c_j \leqslant d$,
\item an arithmetic progression $\mathcal P \subseteq [N]$ with $\# \mathcal P \geqslant N/M$,
\item and decompositions
\[
1_\mathcal A = f + f_{\mathrm{unf}},
\qquad
f1_\mathcal P = f_{\mathrm{str}} + f_{\mathrm{sml}},
\]
\end{enumerate}
such that
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $f: \mathbb N \to [0,1]$,
\item $f_{\mathrm{unf}}: [N] \to [-1,1]$ with
\[
\sup_{{\alpha},{\beta}} \Big|
\sum_{n \leqslant N} f_{\mathrm{unf}}(n) e({\alpha} n^k + {\beta} n)
\Big| \leqslant \frac{N}{\mathcal F(M)},
\]
\item $f_{\mathrm{sml}}: \mathcal P \to [-2, 2]$ with $\| f_{\mathrm{sml}} \|_2 \leqslant {\varepsilon} \| 1_\mathcal P \|_2$,
\item $f_{{\mathrm{str}}}: \mathcal P \to [0,1]$ with $\| f_{\mathrm{str}} \|_1 \gg {\delta} \| 1_\mathcal P \|_1$,
\item as well as a trigonometric polynomial $F: \mathbb T^{c_1 + c_k} \to [0,1]$ of degree at most $M$ such that
\[
f_{\mathrm{str}}(n) = F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} n, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)} n^k)
\qquad (n \in \mathcal P).
\]
\end{enumerate}

label: properties
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{properties}
Let $f,g: [N] \to \mathbb C$, $\phi: [N] \to \mathbb T^d$, and ${\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \in \mathbb T^d$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $(f+g)_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} = f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} + g_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}$.
\item $\langle f, g_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \rangle = \langle f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, g \rangle$.
\item If, for each ${\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}$, the restriction $f\vert_{B_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}({\varepsilon})}$ is constant, then $f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} = f$.
\item $f - f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}$ is orthogonal to any function that is constant on every $B_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}})$.
\end{enumerate}

label: RTinv
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{RTinv}
Let $\Phi$ be a closed subset of $\mathbb T^N$, let $\mathcal I \subseteq \mathbb T$ be an interval of length ${\lambda}(\mathcal I) \leqslant 1/2$, and let $f: \mathbb N \to \mathbb C$. Then there exists $\phi \in \Phi$ such that
\[
\int_\mathbb T \Big|
\sum_{n \in [N]} f(n) 1_{{\alpha} - \mathcal I}(\phi(n)) \Big| \mathrm{d} {\alpha} \geqslant {\lambda}(\mathcal I) \| f \|_\Phi / 2.
\]
head: environment
name: Random translate inverse theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
The map
\[
\mathbb T^N \to \mathbb R, \qquad
\phi \mapsto \Big| \sum_{n \in [N]} f(n) e(\phi(n)) \Big|
\]
is continuous. Hence, by compactness of $\Phi$, there exists $\phi \in \Phi$ such that
\[
\| f \|_\Phi = \Big| \sum_{n \in [N]} f(n) e(\phi(n)) \Big|.
\]
Let us choose representatives $a, b \in \mathbb R$ with $b - a = {\lambda}(\mathcal I)$ such that, viewed as subsets of $\mathbb T$,
\[
(a,b) \subseteq \mathcal I \subseteq [a,b].
\]
For $x \in \mathbb T$,
\[
\int_\mathbb T 1_{x - \mathcal I} ({\alpha}) e({\alpha}) \mathrm{d} {\alpha} = \frac{e(x-a) - e(x-b)}{2 \pi i} = \frac{e(-a) - e(-b)}{2 \pi i} e(x) .
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
\Big| \sum_{n \in [N]} f(n) e(\phi(n)) \Big| 
&= \frac{2 \pi}{|e(b-a) - 1|}  \Big| \sum_{n \in [N]} f(n) \int_\mathbb T 1_{\phi(n)-\mathcal I}({\alpha}) e({\alpha}) \mathrm{d} {\alpha}
\Big|
\\ &\leqslant \frac{2 \pi}{|e(b-a) - 1|} \int_\mathbb T \Big| \sum_{n \in [N]} f(n) 1_{{\alpha} - \mathcal I}(\phi(n)) \Big| \mathrm{d} {\alpha}.
\end{align*}
The conclusion now follows from the fact that
\[
|e(b-a)-1| = 2|\sin(\pi(b-a))| \geqslant 4 \| b - a \|.
\]

label: WR
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Weak regularity

label: EnergyIncrement
title: Proof
body_md:
We perform an iterative procedure. Stage $d \geqslant 0$ begins with $\phi \in \Phi^d$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{EnergyIncrement}
\int_{\mathbb T^d} \| f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \|_2^2 \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \geqslant d({\varepsilon}/4)^2 N.
\end{equation}
We initialise at stage $d = 0$ with $f_0 = \mathbb E_{[N]} f$. The process terminates if $\| f - f_\phi \|_\Phi \leqslant {\varepsilon} N$.

Otherwise $\| f - f_\phi \|_\Phi > {\varepsilon} N$ and, by Lemma \ref{RTinv}, there exists $\phi' \in \Phi$ such that
\[
\int_\mathbb T |
\langle f - f_\phi, g \rangle
| \mathrm{d} {\alpha}'
> {\varepsilon} N/4,
\]
where $g = 1_{{\alpha}' + [0,1/2)} \circ \phi'$.
Thus, by the definition \eqref{BRTproj} of $f_\phi$, linearity, and the triangle inequality,
\[
\int_\mathbb T \int_{\mathbb T^d} | \langle f-f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} , g \rangle | \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \mathrm{d} {\alpha}' > {\varepsilon} N / 4.
\]

Since $g$ and $f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}$ are constant on sets of the form $B_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\alpha}'} ({\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}, {\varepsilon}')$, Lemma \ref{properties} and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
g_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\alpha}'} = g, \qquad
(f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}})_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\alpha}'} = f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},
\]
and
\begin{align*}
|\langle f - f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, g \rangle| &=
|\langle f - f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, g_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\alpha}'} \rangle|
= |\langle f_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},{\alpha}'} - f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, g \rangle|
\leqslant N^{1/2} \| f_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},{\alpha}'} -f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \|_2.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\[
\int_\mathbb T \int_{\mathbb T^d} \| f_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},{\alpha}'} -f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \|_2 \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \mathrm{d} {\alpha}' > {\varepsilon} N^{1/2}/4.
\]
A further application of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality yields
\[
\int_\mathbb T \int_{\mathbb T^d} \| f_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},{\alpha}'} -f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \|_2^2 \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \mathrm{d} {\alpha}' > ({\varepsilon}/4)^2 N.
\]

By Lemma \ref{properties},
\[
\langle f_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\alpha}'} - f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \rangle =
\langle f_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\alpha}'} - (f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}})_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},{\alpha}'}, f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \rangle = \langle f - f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \rangle = 0.
\]
Hence, by Pythagoras's theorem,
\[
\| f_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\alpha}'} \|_2^2 = \| f_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},{\alpha}'} -f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \|_2^2 + \| f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \|_2^2.
\]
Now
\[
\int_\mathbb T \int_{\mathbb T^d} \| f_{\phi,\phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},{\alpha}'} \|_2^2 \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \mathrm{d} {\alpha}' > ({\varepsilon}/4)^2 N + \int_{\mathbb T^d} \| f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \|_2^2 \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}},
\]
so we have \eqref{EnergyIncrement} with $f_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\alpha}'}$ in place of $f_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}$ and $d + 1$ in place of $d$, and we proceed to stage $d+1$.

The left hand side of \eqref{EnergyIncrement} is bounded above by $N$, so our procedure must terminate at some stage $d \leqslant (4/{\varepsilon})^2$ with a projection satisfying \eqref{WRerror}.

label: SFR
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{SFR}
Let $\mathcal F: [1,\infty) \to [1,\infty)$ and ${\varepsilon} > 0$. Let $\Phi$ be a closed subset of $\mathbb T^{N}$ containing zero, and let $f: [N] \to \mathbb C$ be $1$-bounded. Then there exist
\[
1 \leqslant d, d' \ll_{\mathcal F,{\varepsilon}} 1, \qquad \phi \in \Phi^d, \qquad
\phi' \in \Phi^{d'}
\]
such that
\[
\| f - f_{\phi, \phi'} \|_{\Phi} \leqslant N/\mathcal F(d), \qquad
\| f_{\phi, \phi'} - f_{\phi} \|_2 \leqslant {\varepsilon} \sqrt{N}.
\]
head: environment
name: Full regularity

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply Lemma \ref{WR}, furnishing $d_1 \leqslant 16 \mathcal F(0)^2$ and $\phi \in \Phi^{d_1}$ such that
\[
\| f - f_{\phi} \|_{\Phi} \leqslant N/\mathcal F(0).
\]
With $d_2 = 16 \mathcal F(d_1)^2$, Lemma \ref{RWR} gives $\phi' \in \Phi^{d_2}$ such that
\[
\| f - f_{\phi, \phi'} \|_{\Phi} \leqslant N / \mathcal F(d_1).
\]
Iterating this procedure, at stage $j$ we obtain 
\[
d_j = 16 \mathcal F(d_1 + \cdots + d_{j-1})^2, \qquad
\phi \in \Phi^{d_1 + \cdots + d_{j-1}}, \qquad \phi' \in \Phi^{d_j}
\]
such that
\[
\| f - f_{\phi, \phi'} \|_{\Phi} \leqslant N/\mathcal F(d_1 + \cdots + d_{j-1}).
\]

By Lemma \ref{properties} and Pythagoras's theorem, the quantity
\[
\int_{\mathbb T^{d_1 + \cdots + d_j}} \| f_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}'} \|_2^2 \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}' 
= \int_{\mathbb T^{d_1 + \cdots + d_j}} 
(\| f_{\phi}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}} \|_2^2 +  \| f_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}'} - f_{\phi}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}} \|_2^2)
\mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}'
\]
is non-decreasing at each stage of the iteration. As $N$ is an upper bound for this quantity, it follows that at some stage $j \ll_{{\varepsilon}} 1$,
\[
\int_{\mathbb T^{d_1 + \cdots + d_j}} \| f_{\phi, \phi'}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}, {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}'} - f_{\phi}^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}} \|_2^2
\mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}' \leqslant {\varepsilon}^2 N.
\]
The result now follows from the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.
head: environment

label: SymDif
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us represent each ${\gamma}_j \in \mathbb T$ by a real number ${\gamma}_j$ with $|{\gamma}_j| \leqslant 1/2$. As $0 < {\varepsilon} \leqslant 1/2$,
\[
\operatorname{meas}_{\mathbb T^d}
([0,{\varepsilon})^d {\Delta} ([0,{\varepsilon})^d + {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}))
=
\operatorname{meas}_{\mathbb R^d}
([0,{\varepsilon})^d {\Delta} ([0,{\varepsilon})^d + {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}})).
\]

Next, we bound $\operatorname{meas}_{\mathbb R^d}
([0,{\varepsilon})^d \cap ([0,{\varepsilon})^d + {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}))$ from below. This intersection is a box whose $j^{\mathrm{th}}$ side has length $({\varepsilon} - |{\gamma}_j|)_+$ for each $j$, with the notation $x_+ = \max \{ 0, x \}$. Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{meas}_{\mathbb R^d}
([0,{\varepsilon})^d \cap ([0,{\varepsilon})^d + {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}})) = ({\varepsilon} - |{\gamma}_1|)_+ \cdots ({\varepsilon} - |{\gamma}_d|)_+.
\]
We now induct on $d$ to show that this is bounded below by ${\varepsilon}^d - {\varepsilon}^{d-1} \displaystyle \sum_{j \in [d]} |{\gamma}_j|$. This is clear for $d=1$. For $d \geqslant 2$, we compute using the inductive hypothesis that
\begin{align*}
({\varepsilon} - |{\gamma}_1|)_+ \cdots ({\varepsilon} - |{\gamma}_d|)_+
&\geqslant ({\varepsilon} - |{\gamma}_1|)_+ \cdots ({\varepsilon} - |{\gamma}_{d-1}|)_+ {\varepsilon} 
- {\varepsilon}^{d-1} |{\gamma}_d| \\
&\geqslant {\varepsilon}^d - {\varepsilon}^{d-1} \sum_{j \in [d-1]} |{\gamma}_j| - {\varepsilon}^{d-1} |{\gamma}_d| \\
&= {\varepsilon}^d - {\varepsilon}^{d-1} \sum_{j \in [d]} |{\gamma}_j|.
\end{align*}

The upshot is that
\[
\operatorname{meas}_{\mathbb R^d}
([0,{\varepsilon})^d \cap ([0,{\varepsilon})^d + {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}})) \geqslant {\varepsilon}^d - {\varepsilon}^{d-1} \sum_{j \in [d]} |{\gamma}_j|.
\]
The conclusion now follows from the inclusion-exclusion formula for the symmetric difference.

label: Lip
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lip}
Let $\phi: [N] \to \mathbb T^d$, and let $f: [N] \to \mathbb C$ be $1$-bounded. Then there exists a $1$-bounded and $4$-Lipschitz function $F: \mathbb T^d \to \mathbb C$ such that $f_\phi = F \circ \phi$, and if $f \geqslant 0$ then $F \geqslant 0$.
head: environment
name: Lipschitz structure

title: Proof
body_md:
For ${\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \in \{ 0, 1 \}^d$ and ${\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \in \mathbb T^d$, define
\[
F_{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) =
\begin{cases}
        
                                                                  
   
                                                                                                                 
\mathbb E_{m\in B_\phi^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}}({\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}})}f(m),  &\text{if } B_\phi^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}}({\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}) \neq \emptyset, \\
0, &\text{if } B_\phi^{{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}}({\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}) = \emptyset.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \in \{0,1\}^d} \left( 1_{{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}/2 + [0,1/2)^d} * F_{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \right) (\phi(n)) \\
&= \int_{\mathbb T^d} \sum_{{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \in \{0,1\}^d} 1_{{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}/2 + [0,1/2)^d}(\phi(n)-{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) F_{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \\
&= \int_{\mathbb T^d} \sum_{{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \in \{0,1\}^d} 1_{n \in B_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}})} F_{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}
= \int_{\mathbb T^d} \mathbb E_{m \in B_\phi^{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}(n)} f(m) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} = f_\phi(n).
\end{align*}
We define the $1$-bounded function
\[
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \sum_{{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \in \{0,1\}^d} \left( 1_{{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}/2 + [0,1/2)^d} * F_{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \right) ({\boldsymbol{\beta}})  = \sum_{{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \in \{0,1\}^d} \left( 1_{[0,1/2)^d} * F_{\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}} \right) ({\boldsymbol{\beta}} - {\boldsymbol {\varepsilon}}/2),
\]
noting that $f_\phi = F \circ \phi$.

To show that $F$ is $4$-Lipschitz, it suffices to prove that if $G: \mathbb T^d \to \mathbb C$ is $1$-bounded and measurable then $1_{[0,1/2)^d} * G$ is $2^{2-d}$-Lipschitz. This follows from the triangle inequality, a change of variables, and Lemma \ref{SymDif}. Indeed, if ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}, {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}} \in \mathbb T^d$ then
\begin{align*}
&|1_{[0,1/2)^d} * G ({\boldsymbol{\beta}} + {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}) - 1_{[0,1/2)^d} * G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})|
\\
&\leqslant \int_{\mathbb T^d}
|1_{[0,1/2)^d}({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} + {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}) - 1_{[0,1/2)^d}({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}})| \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \\
&= \operatorname{meas}_{\mathbb T^d}(
[0,1/2)^d \Delta
([0,1/2)^d - {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}})) \leqslant 2^{2-d} \sum_{j \in [d]} \| {\gamma}_j \|_\mathbb T.
\end{align*}

label: trig
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{trig}
Let $K \geqslant 1$ and $0 < {\varepsilon} < 1/2$, and let $F: \mathbb T^d \to \mathbb C$ be a $K$-Lipschitz function. Then there exists a $1$-bounded trigonometric polynomial $F_{\varepsilon}: \mathbb T^d \to \mathbb C$ of degree $O(K^2 d^2 {\varepsilon}^{-3})$ such that $\| F - F_{\varepsilon} \|_\infty \leqslant {\varepsilon}$, and if $0 \leqslant F \leqslant 1$ then $0 \leqslant F_{\varepsilon} \leqslant 1$.
head: environment
name: Trigonometric approximation

label: decay
title: Proof
body_md:
For $M \in \mathbb N$, we introduce the Fej\'er kernel
\begin{align*}
\mu_M({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) &= \mu_M({\alpha}_1) \cdots \mu_M({\alpha}_d) \\
&= \sum_{\mathbf m \in \mathbb Z^d} (1-|m_1|/M)_+ \cdots (1-|m_d|/M)_+ e(\mathbf m \cdot {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}),
\end{align*}
where
\[
\mu_M({\alpha}) =
M^{-1}  \left( \frac{\sin M \pi {\alpha}}{\sin \pi {\alpha}} \right)^2.
\]
This has the following properties:
\[
\mu_M \geqslant 0, \qquad
\int_{\mathbb T^d} \mu_M = 1,
\]
and
\begin{equation}
\label{decay}
\mu_M({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) \leqslant 4M^{-1} \| {\alpha}_j \|^{-2} \prod_{i \ne j} \mu_M({\alpha}_i) \qquad (1 \leqslant j \leqslant d).
\end{equation}

For $M = \lceil 1000 (Kd)^2 {\varepsilon}^{-3} \rceil$, we choose
\[
F_{\varepsilon}({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) = F * \mu_M({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) = \int_{\mathbb T^d}  F({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} - {\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \mu_M({\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}.
\]
By orthogonality,
\[
F_{\varepsilon}({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) = \sum_{\mathbf m \in \mathbb Z^d} (1 - |m_1|/M)_+ \cdots (1-|m_d|/M)_+ \hat F(\mathbf m) e(\mathbf m \cdot {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}})
\]
is a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $M$. Moreover, the definition of $F_{\varepsilon}$ as a convolution ensures that if $0 \leqslant F \leqslant 1$ then $0 \leqslant F_{\varepsilon} \leqslant 1$.

Finally, we bound
\[
F({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) - F_{\varepsilon}({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) = \int_{\mathbb T^d} (F({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) - F({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} - {\boldsymbol{\beta}})) \mu_M({\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}.
\]
Let $\eta > 0$ be a threshold given by $\eta^{-3} = KdM$.
As $F$ is $K$-Lipschitz,
\[
\Big|
\int_{\| {\boldsymbol{\beta}} \|_\infty \leqslant \eta} (F({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) - F({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} - {\boldsymbol{\beta}})) \mu_M({\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\Big| \leqslant K d\eta = (Kd)^{2/3} M^{-1/3}.
\]
By \eqref{decay},
\[
\Big|
\int_{\| {\boldsymbol{\beta}} \|_\infty > \eta} (F({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}) - F({\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} - {\boldsymbol{\beta}})) \mu_M({\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\Big| \leqslant 4/(M\eta^2) = 4 (Kd)^{2/3} M^{-1/3}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\| F - F_{\varepsilon} \|_\infty
\leqslant 5 (Kd)^{2/3} M^{-1/3} \leqslant {\varepsilon}.
\]

label: Ratner
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Ratner}
Let ${\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb T^{d_j}$ for $j \in [J]$, where $d_j\geqslant 0$. Put $D = d_1 + \cdots + d_J$, and let $N_1, \ldots, N_J, M_0, \ldots, M_{D} \geqslant 1$. Then there are decompositions
\[
{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)} = \mathbf a^{(j)}/q + {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)}/N_j + L_j {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)} \qquad (1 \leqslant j \leqslant J),
\]
where, for some $0 \leqslant n \leqslant D$ and all $j \in [J]$, we have:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $q \in \mathbb N$ with $q \leqslant M_0\cdots M_{n-1}$
\item $\mathbf a^{(j)} \in \mathbb Z^{d_j}$
\item ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb R^{d_j}$ with $\| {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \|_1 \leqslant \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} M_0\cdots M_{i}$
\item ${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)}$ is $(M_n, N_j)$-irrational with ${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb T^{c_j}$ for some $0 \leqslant c_j \leqslant d_j$
\item $L_j$ is a $d_j \times c_j$ integer matrix whose rows and columns are bounded in $L^1$ by $M_0\cdots M_{n-1}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The inductive base case $D = 0$ is vacuously true, upon interpreting 
$R^0 = \{ 0 \}$ for any ring $R$. Next, let $D \geqslant 1$ and assume the conclusion with $D - 1$ in place of $D$.

If ${\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)}$ is $(M_0, N_j)$-irrational for every $j$, then we can take
\[
n = 0, \quad
q = 1, \quad
\mathbf a^{(j)} = {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} = \mathbf 0, \quad
L_j = I_{d_j},
\quad
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)} = {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)}.
\]
Thus, we may assume instead that there exist $i \in [J]$, as well as $\mathbf 0 \ne \mathbf q \in \mathbb Z^{d_i}$ such that
\[
\| \mathbf q \|_1 \leqslant M_0,
\qquad
\| \mathbf q \cdot {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(i)} \| \leqslant M_0 / N_i.
\]
It follows on viewing ${\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(i)}$ as a real vector that
\[
\mathbf q \cdot {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(i)} = a + {\beta} / N_i,
\]
for some $a \in \mathbb Z$ and some ${\beta} \in \mathbb R$ with $|{\beta}| \leqslant M_0$. Relabelling indices if necessary, we may assume that the first co-ordinate of $\mathbf q$, denoted $q_1$, is non-zero. Now
\[
{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(i)} - (a/q_1 + {\beta}/(q_1 N_i), 0, \ldots, 0)
\]
lies in the kernel of the real linear transformation $\mathbf v \mapsto \mathbf q \cdot \mathbf v$. This kernel is given by $L \cdot \mathbb R^{d_i - 1}$, where
\[
L = \begin{pmatrix}
q_2 & \ldots & q_{d_i} \\
-q_1 & & \\
& \ddots & \\
&& - q_1
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is a $d_i \times (d_i  - 1)$ integer matrix. Thus, we may write
\[
{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(i)} - (a/q_1 + {\beta}/(q_1 N_i), 0, \ldots, 0)
= L \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(i)},
\]
for some $\tilde {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(i)} \in \mathbb T^{d_i - 1}$.

Put $\tilde d_i = d_i - 1$.
Setting $\tilde {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)} = {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)}$ and $\tilde d_j = d_j$ for $j \ne i$, the induction hypothesis --- applied to $M_1, \ldots, M_D$ --- furnishes decompositions
\[
\tilde {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)} = \tilde \mathbf a^{(j)} / \tilde q + \tilde {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} / N_j + \tilde L_j {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)}
\]
where, for some $1 \leqslant n \leqslant D$ and all $j \in [J]$, we have:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\tilde q \in \mathbb N$ with $\tilde q \leqslant M_1\cdots M_{n-1}$
\item $\tilde \mathbf a^{(j)} \in \mathbb Z^{\tilde d_j}$
\item $\tilde {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb R^{\tilde d_j}$, where 
$
\| \tilde {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \|_1 \leqslant \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}M_1\cdots M_{i}
$
\item ${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)}$ is $(M_n, N_j)$-irrational with ${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb T^{\tilde c_j}$ for some $0 \leqslant \tilde c_j \leqslant \tilde d_j$ 
\item $\tilde L_j$ a $\tilde d_j \times \tilde c_j$ integer matrix whose rows and columns are bounded in $L^1$ by $M_1\cdots M_{n-1}$.
\end{enumerate}
Now
\[
{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(i)} = (a/q_1 + {\beta}/(q_1 N_i), 0, \ldots, 0) + L(\tilde \mathbf a^{(i)}/ \tilde q + \tilde {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(i)}/ N_i + \tilde L_i {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(i)}),
\]
and the claims follow from the inductive data upon choosing
\begin{align*}
q &= |q_1| \tilde q,
\\
\mathbf a^{(i)} &= (\tilde q a |q_1|/q_1, 0, \ldots, 0) + L |q_1| \tilde \mathbf a^{(i)},
\\
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(i)} &= ({\beta}/q_1,0,\ldots,0) + L \tilde {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(i)}, \\ 
L_i &= L \tilde L_i,
\end{align*}
as well as
\[
\mathbf a^{(j)} = |q_1| \tilde \mathbf a^{(j)}, \quad
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} = \tilde {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)}, \quad
L_j = \tilde L_j
\qquad (j \ne i).
\]

label: pigeonhole
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{pigeonhole}
Let ${\varepsilon}, {\delta} > 0$. Let $f: [N] \to [-1,1]$ and $g: [N] \to [0,\infty)$ with
\[
\sum_{n \in [N]} f(n) \geqslant {\delta} N, \qquad
\sum_{n \in [N]} g(n) \leqslant {\varepsilon} N.
\]
Then, for any partition $[N] = \mathcal C_1 \cup \cdots \cup \mathcal C_r$, there exists $i \in [r]$ such that
\[
|\mathcal C_i| \geqslant {\delta} N / (3r),
\qquad
\sum_{n \in \mathcal C_i} f(n) \geqslant {\delta} |\mathcal C_i|/3, \qquad
\sum_{n \in \mathcal C_i} g(n) \leqslant 3 {\delta}^{-1} {\varepsilon} |\mathcal C_i|.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Observe that
\[
\sum_{i \in [r]} \Bigl(
\Bigl(
\sum_{n \in \mathcal C_i} f(n)
\Bigr)
- \frac{{\delta} |\mathcal C_i|}{3} - \frac{{\delta}}{3 {\varepsilon}} \sum_{n \in \mathcal C_i} g(n) \Bigr) \geqslant \frac{{\delta}}{3} N.
\]
Thus, by the greedy algorithm, there exists $i \in [r]$ such that
\[
\Bigl(
\sum_{n \in \mathcal C_i} f(n)
\Bigr)
- \frac{{\delta} |\mathcal C_i|}{3} - \frac{{\delta}}{3 {\varepsilon}} \sum_{n \in \mathcal C_i} g(n) \geqslant \frac{{\delta}}{3r} N.
\]
Now
\[
|\mathcal C_i| \geqslant \sum_{n \in \mathcal C_i} f(n) \geqslant \frac{{\delta} |\mathcal C_i|}{3} + \frac{{\delta}}{3 {\varepsilon}} \sum_{n \in \mathcal C_i} g(n) + \frac{{\delta}}{3r} N.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $c = c(\boldsymbol \Psi)$ be a sufficiently small, positive constant, and put $\eta = c {\varepsilon} {\delta}$.
                                                                                                                   
By replacing $\mathcal F(x)$ by $\max \{ \mathcal F(y): 1 \leqslant y \leqslant x \}$, we may assume that $\mathcal F$ is non-decreasing and defined on $[1, \infty)$.
Define, for $x \in \mathbb N$,
                
              
                  
              
\begin{align*}
\mathcal F_0(x) &= 
\mathcal F(\eta ^{-4}x^{2}), \\
\mathcal F_j(x) &= \mathcal F \Bigl(
\eta ^{-4}x^{2} \Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\mathcal F_{0}(x)\cdots \mathcal F_i(x)\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr) \qquad (1 \leqslant j \leqslant Jx),
\\
\mathcal F_*(x) &= \mathcal F_{Jx}(x).
\end{align*}

We apply Lemma \ref{SFR} to the function $g \coloneq 1_{\mathcal A}$, with $\Phi = \mathbb T\textnormal{-span}(\boldsymbol \Psi)$, growth function $\mathcal F_*$ and approximation parameter $\eta > 0$. This yields positive integers $d, \tilde d \ll_{\mathcal F,{\varepsilon},{\delta},\boldsymbol \Psi} 1$, as well as  
$
{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb T^d
$
and
$
\tilde {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb T^{\tilde d}
$
such that
\[
\phi \coloneq {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(1)} \Psi_1 + \cdots + {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(J)} \Psi_J,
\qquad
\tilde \phi \coloneq
\tilde {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(1)}\Psi_1 + \cdots + \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(J)} \Psi_J
\]
satisfy
\[
\| g - g_{\phi, \tilde \phi} \|_{\Phi} \leqslant N/\mathcal F_*(d), \qquad
\| g_{\phi, \tilde \phi} - g_{\phi} \|_2 \leqslant \eta \sqrt N.
\]
Define $f, f_{{\mathrm{unf}}}, g_{{\mathrm{str}}}, g_{{\mathrm{sml}}}: [N] \to [-1,1]$ by
\begin{gather}
f = g_{\phi,\tilde \phi}, \qquad
f_{\mathrm{unf}} = g - f, \\
g_{\mathrm{str}} = g_{\phi}, \qquad
g_{\mathrm{sml}} = f - g_{\mathrm{str}}.
\end{gather}
Then we have
\begin{gather}
f \geqslant 0, \qquad
\| f_{\mathrm{unf}} \|_{\Phi} \leqslant N/\mathcal F_*(d), \\
\sum_{n \in [N]} g_{\mathrm{str}}(n) \geqslant {\delta} N, \qquad
\sum_{n \in [N]} |g_{\mathrm{sml}}(n)|^2 \leqslant \eta^2 N.
\end{gather}
Moreover, Lemma \ref{Lip} provides a $4$-Lipschitz function $G: \mathbb T^d \to [0,1]$ such that
\[
g_{{\mathrm{str}}}(n) = G(\phi(n)) \qquad (1 \leqslant n \leqslant N).
\]

Next, we apply Lemma \ref{Ratner} with
\[
M_n = \mathcal F_n(d)
\quad (0 \leqslant n \leqslant D), \qquad
D = Jd.
\]
Thus there is $0\leqslant n \leqslant D$ and decompositions
\[
{\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}}^{(j)} = \mathbf a^{(j)}/q + {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)}/N^{k_j} + L_j {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)}
\qquad (1 \leqslant j \leqslant J),
\]
such that on setting
\begin{equation}
Q = 
\begin{cases}
1,& \text{if } n = 0, \\
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \mathcal F_0(d)\cdots \mathcal F_i(d),&\text{if } n \ne 0,
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
we have:
\begin{itemize}
\item $q \in \mathbb N$ with $q \leqslant Q$
\item $\mathbf a^{(j)} \in \mathbb Z^d$
\item ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb R^d$ with $\| {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \|_1 \leqslant Q$
\item ${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)}$ is $(\mathcal F_n(d), N^{k_j})$-irrational with
${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)} \in \mathbb T^{c_j}$ for some $c_j \leqslant d$
\item $L_j$ is a $d \times c_j$ integer matrix whose rows and columns are bounded in $L^1$ by $Q$.
\end{itemize}

We partition $[N]$ into $O(qQ/\eta)$ many arithmetic progressions of common difference $q$ and diameter at most $\eta N / Q$. By Lemma \ref{pigeonhole}, there exists an arithmetic progression $\mathcal P \subseteq [N]$ of common difference $q$ such that
\begin{align*}
|\mathcal P| &\gg {\delta} \eta N / (qQ), \\
\sum_{n \in \mathcal P} g_{\mathrm{str}}(n) &\gg {\delta} |\mathcal P|, \\
\sum_{n \in \mathcal P} |g_{\mathrm{sml}}(n)|^2 &\ll {\delta}^{-1} \eta^2 |\mathcal P|.
\end{align*}

Fix $b \in \mathcal P$ arbitrarily, and define
$
\tilde G: \mathbb T^{c_1} \times \cdots \times \mathbb T^{c_J}
\to [0,1]
$
by
\[
\tilde G ({\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(1)}, \cdots, {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(J)}) =
G \Bigl(
\sum_{j \in [J]}
(\mathbf a^{(j)} \Psi_j(b)/q + {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \Psi_j(b)/N^{k_j} +  L_j {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(j)})
\Bigr).
\]
Recall that $G$ is $4$-Lipschitz so, for $n \in \mathcal P$,
\begin{align*}
g_{\mathrm{str}}(n) &=
 G  \Bigl(
\sum_{j \in [J]}
(\mathbf a^{(j)} \Psi_j(n)/q + {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \Psi_j(n)/N^{k_j} + \Psi_j(n) L_j {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)})
\Bigr)
\\
&=  G \Bigl(
\sum_{j \in [J]}
(\mathbf a^{(j)} \Psi_j(b)/q + {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(j)} \Psi_j(n)/N^{k_j} + \Psi_j(n) L_j {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(j)})
\Bigr)
\\
&= \tilde G ({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} \Psi_1(n), \ldots, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(J)} \Psi_J(n))
+ O_{\boldsymbol \Psi}(\eta).
\end{align*}
Moreover $\tilde G$ is $4Q$-Lipschitz so, by Lemma \ref{trig}, there exists a trigonometric polynomial 
\[
F: \mathbb T^{c_1} \times \cdots \times \mathbb T^{c_J} \to [0,1]
\]
of degree $O(Q^2 (Jd)^2 \eta^{-3})$ such that $\| \tilde G - F \|_\infty \leqslant \eta$. We define, for $n \in \mathcal P$,
\begin{align*}
f_{\mathrm{str}}(n) &=
F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} \Psi_1(n), \ldots, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(J)} \Psi_J(n)),
\\
f_{\mathrm{sml}}(n) &=
(g_{\mathrm{sml}} + g_{\mathrm{str}} - f_{\mathrm{str}})(n).
\end{align*}

Next, we verify the first list of  assertions.
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item These hold with the choice $M = \lfloor Q^{2} d^2\eta^{-4} \rfloor$.
\item This holds because
$\mathcal F_n(d) \geqslant \mathcal F(M)$.
\item This holds because $|\mathcal P| \gg {\delta} \eta N / (qQ)$ and $c$ is sufficiently small.
\item The two equations hold by construction.
\end{enumerate}
Finally, we verify the second list of  assertions.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item We have already observed this.
\item This holds because
$\mathcal F_*(d)\geqslant \mathcal F_n(d) \geqslant \mathcal F(M)$.
        
 
                                    
 
   
\item As
$
\| f_{\mathrm{sml}} - g_{\mathrm{sml}} \|_{L^\infty(\mathcal P)} \ll_{\boldsymbol \Psi} \eta$ and
$\| g_{\mathrm{sml}} 1_{\mathcal P} \|_2 \ll {\delta}^{-1/2} \eta \| 1_\mathcal P \|_2,
$
the triangle inequality implies
$
\| f_{\mathrm{sml}} \|_2 \ll {\delta}^{-1/2} \eta \| 1_{\mathcal P} \|_2.
$
Since $c$ is small and ${\delta} \leqslant 1$, it follows that $\|f_{\mathrm{sml}}\|_2 \leqslant {\varepsilon} \| 1_{\mathcal P} \|_2$.
\item As $\|f_{\mathrm{str}} - g_{\mathrm{str}}\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal P)} \ll_{\boldsymbol \Psi} \eta$ and $\| g_{\mathrm{str}} 1_{\mathcal P} \|_1 \gg {\delta} |\mathcal P|$, the triangle inequality gives $\| f_{\mathrm{str}} \|_1 \gg {\delta} |\mathcal P|$.
\item The degree is bounded by $M$ because $c$ is sufficiently small.
\end{enumerate}

title: Remark
body_md:
Let us view $\mathbf x \in \mathcal P^s$ as a random variable. Put 
\[
\mathbf u = (u,\ldots,u), \qquad \mathbf u + m \mathbf z = \mathbf x = (R-y_1,\ldots, R-y_s),
\]
and note from \eqref{zerosum} that $\mathfrak F(1,\ldots,1) = \mathfrak L(1,\ldots,1) = 0$. As
\[
\mathfrak F(\mathbf x) = \mathfrak F(\mathbf u + m \mathbf z) \equiv 0 \: \mathrm{mod} \: g^{k-1} m
\]
and
\[
\mathfrak F(\mathbf x) = \mathfrak F(R-y_1,\ldots,R-y_s) \ll R^{k-1} (R-L),
\]
the probability that $\mathfrak F(\mathbf x) = 0$ is roughly
\[
\frac{g^{k-1}m} { R^{k-1} (R-L)},
\]
and similarly the probability that $\mathfrak L(\mathbf x) = 0$ is $m/(R-L)$. 

There is an extra congruence in Case \ref{case:eq}:
\[
\mathfrak F(\mathbf u+m\mathbf z) \equiv ku^{k-1} L(\mathbf u + m\mathbf z) \: \mathrm{mod} \: g^{k-2} m^2.
\]
There is also an extra archimedean factor in Case \ref{case:eq}, for if $\mathfrak L(\mathbf x) = 0$ then
\[
\mathfrak F(\mathbf x) = \mathfrak F(R-y_1,\ldots,R-y_s) \ll R^{k-2}(R-L)^2.
\]
Thus, we expect roughly
\[
\frac{g^{k-1} m^2 \# \mathcal P^s}{R^{k-1}(R-L)^2} \sim \frac{g^{k-1} \# \mathcal P^{s-2}}{R^{k-1}}
\]
many points in $\mathcal V(P)$ in Case \ref{case:neq}, and roughly 
\[
\frac{g^{k-2} \# \mathcal P^{s-3}}{R^{k-2}}
\]
many points in Case \ref{case:eq}.

label: FourierControl
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{FourierControl}
If each $g_i$ is $1$-bounded and
\[
T(\mathbf g) \geqslant {\delta} N^{s-k-1},
\]
for some ${\delta} \in (0,1)$, then
\[
\| \mathbf g \|_{{\mathrm{FL}}} \gg {\delta}^{2s} N^s.
\]
head: environment
name: Fourier control

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $t = s_0 -\frac{1}{2}$. By H\"older's inequality,
\begin{align*}
    {\delta} N^{s-k-1}
    &\leqslant T(\mathbf g)
    =\int_{\mathbb T^2} |\tilde \mathbf g({\alpha},{\beta})| \mathrm{d} {\alpha} \mathrm{d} {\beta} \\
    &\leqslant \| \mathbf g \|_{{\mathrm{FL}}}^{(s-t)/s} \int_{\mathbb T^2} \prod_i | \tilde{g_i}(a_i {\alpha}, b_i {\beta}) |^{t/s} \mathrm{d} {\alpha} \mathrm{d} {\beta} \\
    &\leqslant \| \mathbf g \|_{{\mathrm{FL}}}^{(s-t)/s} \prod_{i \leqslant s} \Bigl( \int_{\mathbb T^2} |\tilde{g_i}(a_i {\alpha}, b_i {\beta})|^{t} \mathrm{d} {\alpha} \mathrm{d} {\beta} \Bigr)^{1/s}.
\end{align*}

First, suppose $k \geqslant 3$. Let $\zeta > 0$ be small in terms of $k$, then for each $i\in [s]$,
\begin{align}
&\int_{\mathbb T^{2}} \abs{\tilde g_i(a_i \alpha, b_i \beta)}^{t} \mathrm{d} \alpha \mathrm{d} \beta 
= 
\int_{\mathbb T^{2}} \abs{\tilde g_i(\alpha, \beta)}^{t} \mathrm{d} \alpha \mathrm{d} \beta    
\\
&\leqslant N^{(1-\zeta)/2} \int_{\mathbb T^{2}} \abs{\tilde g_i(\alpha, \beta)}^{s_0 -1} \mathrm{d} \alpha \mathrm{d} \beta    
+ \int_{\abs{\tilde g_i(\alpha, \beta)} \geqslant N^{1-\zeta}} \abs{\tilde g_i(\alpha, \beta)}^{t} \mathrm{d} \alpha \mathrm{d} \beta.
\end{align}
Observing that $s_0 -1$ is an even integer, by orthogonality and Lemma \ref{lm:moment-bound}, we get
\[
\int_{\mathbb T^2} |\tilde{g_i}({\alpha}, {\beta})|^{s_0 -1} \mathrm{d} {\alpha} \mathrm{d} {\beta} 
\ll N^{s_0 -k - 2 + \varepsilon}.
\]
Moreover, \cite[Theorem 1.4]{HH2018} implies
\begin{equation}
    \int_{\abs{\tilde g_i(\alpha, \beta)} \geqslant N^{1-\zeta}} \abs{\tilde g_i(\alpha, \beta)}^{t} \mathrm{d} \alpha \mathrm{d} \beta
    \ll N^{t -k - 1},
\end{equation}
and thus
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:restricion-estimate}
    \int_{\mathbb T^{2}} \abs{\tilde g_i(a_i \alpha, b_i \beta)}^{t} \mathrm{d} \alpha \mathrm{d} \beta    
    \ll N^{t-k-1}.
\end{equation}
Therefore
\[
    {\delta} N^{s-k- 1} \ll \| \mathbf g \|_{{\mathrm{FL}}}^{(s-t)/s} N^{t-k - 1},
\]
and so
\[
\| \mathbf g \|_{{\mathrm{FL}}} \gg {\delta}^{s/(s-t)} N^s \geqslant {\delta}^{2s} N^s.
\]

Now suppose instead that $k=2$. By \cite[Equation (3.115)]{Bou1993},
\[
    \int_{\mathbb T^2} |\tilde{g_i}(a_i {\alpha}, b_i {\beta})|^{t} \mathrm{d} {\alpha} \mathrm{d} {\beta} 
    = \int_{\mathbb T^2} |\tilde{g_i}({\alpha}, {\beta})|^{t} \mathrm{d} {\alpha} \mathrm{d} {\beta} 
    \ll N^{t -3}
    \qquad (1 \leqslant i \leqslant s).
\]
The argument now follows as above.

label: Weyl
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Weyl}
If
\[
\Big|
\sum_{\mathbf n \in \mathcal P^s} e \Bigl( \sum_{i \leqslant s} ({\alpha}_i n_i^k + {\beta}_i n_i) \Bigr) \Big| \geqslant {\delta} N^s,
\]
then                                                   
:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item each ${\alpha}_i$ is $(O({\delta}^{-O(1)}),N^k)$-rational,
\item each ${\beta}_i$ is $(O({\delta}^{-O(1)}),N)$-rational.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Weyl-type bound

title: Proof
body_md:
By symmetry, it suffices to prove the result for $i=1$. We may assume that $0 < {\delta} < 1/2$, since otherwise we can argue with ${\delta}/3$ in place of ${\delta}$. By the triangle inequality, the assumption implies that
\[
\Big| \sum_{n \in \mathcal P} e({\alpha} n^k + {\beta} n) \Big| \geqslant {\delta} N,
\]
where ${\alpha} = {\alpha}_1$ and ${\beta} = {\beta}_1$. Writing
\[
\mathcal I = \{ y \in \mathbb Z: L < u + m y \leqslant R \}
\]
yields
\[
\Big|
\sum_{y \in \mathcal I} e({\alpha} (u+my)^k + {\beta} my)
\Big| \geqslant {\delta} N.
\]
With 
\[
t = \lfloor (L-u)/m \rfloor, \qquad
z = y - t,
\qquad
\mathcal I' = \mathcal I - t,
\qquad v = u - mt,
\]
we now have
\[
\Big|
\sum_{z \in \mathcal I'}
e({\alpha}(v + mz)^k + {\beta} m z) \Big| \geqslant {\delta} N.
\]
Now \cite[Lemma 4.4]{GT2012} furnishes the $(O({\delta}^{-O(1)}),|\mathcal P|^k)$-rationality of
$m^k {\alpha}$, as well as the $(O({\delta}^{-O(1)}),|\mathcal P|)$-rationality of $km u^{k-1} {\alpha} + m {\beta}$. The result now follows from the triangle inequality and the bounds
\[
u \leqslant m,
\qquad
|\mathcal P| \leqslant N/m.
\]

label: WeylCor
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{WeylCor}
Let $A \geqslant 1$. Suppose that ${\boldsymbol{{\alpha}}} \in \mathbb T$ is $(A,N^k)$-irrational or that ${\beta} \in \mathbb T$ is $(A,N)$-irrational. Then              
\[
\sum_{n \in \mathcal P} e({\alpha} n^k + {\beta} n)
\ll M A^{-{\Omega}(1)} |\mathcal P|.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $c > 0$ be the reciprocal of the largest implied constant appearing in Lemma \ref{Weyl}, and suppose
\[
\Big|
\sum_{n \in \mathcal P} e({\alpha} n^k + {\beta} n) \Big|
\geqslant (cA)^{-c} N.
\]
Applying Lemma \ref{Weyl} with
\[
{\delta} = (cA)^{-c}, \qquad
({\alpha}_i, {\beta}_i) = 
\begin{cases}
({\alpha}, {\beta}), &\text{if } i= 1, \\
(0,0), &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
delivers a contradiction                  
. Thus,                 
\[
\sum_{n \in \mathcal P} e({\alpha} n^k + {\beta} n) \ll A^{-c} N \leqslant M A^{-c} |\mathcal P|.
\]

label: equi1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{equi1}
Let $A \geqslant M$. Let $d_1, d_k \leqslant M$ be positive integers, and put $d = d_1 + d_k$. Let $F: \mathbb T^d \to \mathbb C$ be a $1$-bounded trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $M$. If                        
each ${\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(i)} \in \mathbb T^{d_i}$ is $(A,N^i)$-irrational, then
\[
\displaystyle
\mathbb E_{n \in \mathcal P} F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} n, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)} n^k) = \int_{\mathbb T^d} F({\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}} + O(M^{O(1)} A^{-{\Omega}(1)}).

head: environment
name: Equidistribution I

title: Proof
body_md:
Expanding $F$ as a Fourier series gives
\begin{equation}
\sum_{n \in \mathcal P} F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)}n, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)}n^k)
= \hat F(\mathbf 0) |\mathcal P| + \sum_{0 < \| \mathbf m \|_1 \leqslant M} \hat F(\mathbf m) \sum_{n \in \mathcal P}
e(\mathbf m^{(1)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} n + \mathbf m^{(k)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)} n^k),
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf m = (\mathbf m^{(1)}, \mathbf m^{(k)})$ with $\mathbf m^{(i)} \in \mathbb Z^{d_i}$. Note that $\mathbf m^{(i)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(i)}$ is $(A/M, N^i)$-irrational, for some $i$. Thus, by Corollary \ref{WeylCor},
\[
\sum_{n \in \mathcal P} e(\mathbf m^{(1)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} n + \mathbf m^{(k)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)} n^k) \ll M A^{-{\Omega}(1)} |\mathcal P|.
\]
Substituting this into the Fourier expansion above delivers the claimed estimate.

label: OnMajorArc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{OnMajorArc}
Suppose
\[
|T(1_\mathcal P e_{{\alpha}_1, {\beta}_1}, \ldots, 1_\mathcal P e_{{\alpha}_s, {\beta}_s})| \geqslant {\delta} N^{s-k-1}.
\]
Then                        
, for all $i,j \in [s]$,
\begin{itemize}
\item $a_j {\alpha}_i - a_i {\alpha}_j$ is $(O({\delta}^{-O(1)}), N^k)$-rational
\item $b_j {\beta}_i - b_i {\beta}_j$ is $(O({\delta}^{-O(1)}),N)$-rational.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{FourierControl}, there exist ${\lambda}, \mu \in \mathbb T$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\mathbf n \in \mathcal P^s}
e\Bigl(
\sum_{i \in [s]}
((a_i {\lambda} + {\alpha}_i) n_i^k + (b_i \mu + {\beta}_i) n_i) \Bigr) \gg {\delta}^{O(1)} N^s.
\]
Now Lemma \ref{Weyl} tells us that each $a_i {\lambda} + a_i$ is $(O({\delta}^{-O(1)}),N^k)$-rational. Thus, by the triangle inequality,
\[
a_j {\alpha}_i - a_i {\alpha}_j = a_j( a_i {\gamma} + {\alpha}_i) - a_i (a_j {\alpha} + {\alpha}_j)
\]
is also $(O({\delta}^{-O(1)}),N^k)$-rational. The second assertion follows similarly.

label: CountingEquidistribution
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{CountingEquidistribution}
Let $A \geqslant 1$.
Let ${\alpha}_1, \ldots, {\alpha}_s, {\beta}_1, \ldots, {\beta}_s$ be such that at least one of numbers
\[
a_j {\alpha}_i - a_i {\alpha}_j
\qquad (1 \leqslant i, j \leqslant s)
\]
is $(A,N^k)$-irrational or at least one of the numbers
\[
b_j {\beta}_i - b_i {\beta}_j
\qquad (1 \leqslant i, j \leqslant s)
\]
is $(A,N)$-irrational. Then              
\[
T(1_\mathcal P e_{{\alpha}_1, {\beta}_1}, \ldots, 1_\mathcal P e_{{\alpha}_s, {\beta}_s}) \ll A^{-{\Omega}(1)} N^{s-k-1}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $c > 0$ be the reciprocal of the largest implied constant appearing in Lemma \ref{OnMajorArc}, and suppose
\[
|T(1_\mathcal P e_{{\alpha}_1, {\beta}_1}, \ldots, 1_\mathcal P e_{{\alpha}_s, {\beta}_s})| \geqslant (cA)^{-c} N^{s-k-1}.
\]
Then Lemma \ref{OnMajorArc} yields a contradiction.

label: parallel
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{parallel}
Let $a_1, \ldots, a_s \in \mathbb Z$ with $\gcd(a_1, \ldots, a_s) = 1$, and let $\mathbf m^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf m^{(s)} \in \mathbb Z^d$. Then
\[
a_j \mathbf m^{(i)} = a_i \mathbf m^{(j)} \qquad (1 \leqslant i,j \leqslant s)
\]
holds if and only if there exists $\mathbf m \in \mathbb Z^d$ such that
\[
\mathbf m^{(i)} = a_i \mathbf m
\qquad (1 \leqslant i \leqslant s).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $a_j \mathbf m^{(i)} = a_i \mathbf m^{(j)}$ for all $i$ and $j$. Then $\mathbf m^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf m^{(s)}$ are all proportional to some primitive vector $\mathbf m^{(0)} \in \mathbb Z^d$. For each $i$, let $c_i \in \mathbb Z$ be such that $\mathbf m^{(i)} = c_i \mathbf m^{(0)}$. Then $a_j c_i = a_i c_j$ for all $i$ and $j$, so $\mathbf c = {\lambda} \mathbf a$ for some ${\lambda} \in \mathbb Z$. Choosing $\mathbf m = {\lambda} \mathbf m^{(0)}$ yields $\mathbf m^{(i)} = a_i \mathbf m$ for all $i$.

The converse is clear.

title: Proof
body_md:
Expanding the left hand side into Fourier series gives
    \begin{align}
        &\sum_{\mathbf n \in \mathcal V(\mathcal P)} F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} n_1, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)} n_1^k) \cdots F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} n_s, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)} n_s^k) \\
        &=\sum_{\substack{{\mathbf m^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf m^{(s)} \in \mathbb Z^{d_1}} \\
        {\tilde \mathbf m^{(1)}, \ldots, \tilde \mathbf m^{(s)} \in \mathbb Z^{d_k}}}} \hat F(\mathbf m^{(1)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(1)}) \cdots
        \hat F(\mathbf m^{(s)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(s)}) \\
        &\qquad \qquad
        \cdot T(1_{\mathcal P} e_{\mathbf m^{(1)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)},
            \tilde \mathbf m^{(1)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)}}, \ldots, 1_{\mathcal P} e_{\mathbf m^{(s)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)},
        \tilde \mathbf m^{(s)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)}}).
    \end{align}
As $F$ has degree at most $M$, we note that if $\hat F(\mathbf m^{(i)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(i)}) \ne 0$ then
\[
\| \mathbf m^{(i)} \| + \| \tilde \mathbf m^{(i)} \| \leqslant M.
\]
Observe that if $a_j \tilde \mathbf m^{(i)} \ne a_i \tilde \mathbf m^{(j)}$ then $(a_j \tilde \mathbf m^{(i)} - a_i \tilde \mathbf m^{(j)}) \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)}$ is $(A/(CM), N^k)$-irrational, and if $b_j \mathbf m^{(i)} \ne b_i \mathbf m^{(j)}$ then $(b_j \mathbf m^{(i)} - b_i \mathbf m^{(j)}) \cdot {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)}$ is $(A/(CM), N)$-irrational. Thus, by Corollary \ref{CountingEquidistribution}, we have
\begin{align}
    &\sum_{\mathbf n \in \mathcal V(\mathcal P)} F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} n_1, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)} n_1^k) \cdots F({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(1)} n_s, {\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{(k)} n_s^k) \\
    &= \sum_{(\mathbf m, \tilde \mathbf m) \in \mathcal W} \hat F(\mathbf m^{(1)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(1)}) \cdots
    \hat F(\mathbf m^{(s)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(s)}) T(1_\mathcal P) 
    + O(M^{O(1)} A^{-{\Omega}(1)} N^{s-k-1}),
\end{align}
where $\mathcal W$ is the set of $(\mathbf m, \tilde \mathbf m) \in \mathbb Z^{(d_1+d_k)s}$ such that
\[
a_j \tilde \mathbf m^{(i)} = a_i \tilde \mathbf m^{(j)},
\quad
b_j \mathbf m^{(i)} = b_i \mathbf m^{(j)}
\qquad (1 \leqslant i, j \leqslant s).
\]
Finally, by Lemma \ref{ConstrainedOrth},
\begin{align}
    & \int_{\mathcal K(\mathbf a, d_k)} \int_{\mathcal K(\mathbf b, d_1)} \prod_{i \leqslant s} F({\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(i)}, \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(i)}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}} \mathrm{d} \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}
    \\
    &= 
    \begin{multlined}[t]
        \sum_{(\mathbf m, \tilde \mathbf m) \in \mathbb Z^{(d_1+d_k)s}} 
        \hat F(\mathbf m^{(1)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(1)}) \cdots
        \hat F(\mathbf m^{(s)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(s)})
        \\
        \qquad \qquad \int_{\mathcal K(\mathbf a, d_k)} \int_{\mathcal K(\mathbf b, d_1)}
        e\Bigl(
        \sum_{i \in [s]} \mathbf m^{(i)} \cdot {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(i)} \Bigr)
        e\Bigl(
        \sum_{i \in [s]} \tilde \mathbf m^{(i)} \cdot \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(i)} \Bigr) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}} \mathrm{d} \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}
    \end{multlined} 
 \\ & = \sum_{(\mathbf m, \tilde \mathbf m) \in \mathcal W} \hat F(\mathbf m^{(1)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(1)}) \cdots
 \hat F(\mathbf m^{(s)}, \tilde \mathbf m^{(s)}).
\end{align}

title: Definition
body_md: Given an $r\times m$ integer matrix $M$ and a compact abelian group $G$, we have a continuous homomorphism $G^m \to G^r$ given by ${\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}} \mapsto M {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}$.  The kernel $\ker_G M$ is a compact abelian group and therefore has an associated Haar probability measure $\mu_{\ker_G M}$. We note that if $f : G \to \mathbb C$ is Borel measurable then  ${\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}} \mapsto \prod_{i=1}^s f(\gamma_i)$ is Borel measurable on $G^s$, as is the restriction of this function to $\ker_G M$.

name: Kernel measure

label: compact Roth
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{compact Roth}
Let $M$ be an $r\times m$ integer matrix such that the greatest common divisor of the $r\times r$ minors is $1$. Suppose that the columns of $M$ sum to zero. For any $\delta > 0$, there exists $\eta = \eta(M, \delta) > 0$ such that for any compact abelian group $G$, if $\mathcal A \subseteq G$ is  measurable with $\mu_{G}(\mathcal A) \geqslant \delta$, then 
$$
\mu_{\ker_G M}(\mathcal A^m \cap \ker_G M) \geqslant \eta.
$$

label: CompactRothCor
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{CompactRothCor}
Let $a_i, a_i'$ be integers with $a_1 + \dots + a_s = a_1' + \dots + a_s' = 0$ and $\gcd(a_1, \dots, a_s) = \gcd(a_1', \dots, a_s') = 1$.
For any $\delta > 0$, there exists $\eta = \eta(\mathbf a, \mathbf a', \delta) > 0$ such that if $f: \mathbb T^{d} \times \mathbb T^{d'} \to [0,1]$ is measurable and $\int_{\mathbb T^{d+d'}}  f \geqslant \delta$, then 
$$
\int_{\mathcal K(\mathbf a,d)} \int_{\mathcal K(\mathbf a',d')}\prod_{i=1}^s f({\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(i)}, \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(i)}) \mathrm{d} {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}} \mathrm{d} \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}} \geqslant \eta.
$$

title: Proof
body_md:
We note that the columns of the matrix \eqref{system matrix} sum to zero. Furthermore, the greatest common divisor of the $2 \times 2$ minors is
\[
\gcd(\{
a_ia_j' : 1 \leqslant i, j \leqslant s \}) = 1.
\]
Let
\[
\mathcal A = \{ ({\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}, \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}) \in \mathbb T^{d+d'} : f({\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}, \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}) \geqslant \delta/2 \}.
\]
Then the measure of $\mathcal A$ is at least $\delta/2$, and applying Proposition \ref{compact Roth} with $G = \mathbb T^{d+d'}$ gives
$$
\mu_{\ker_{G}M }(\mathcal A^s\cap \ker_G M) \gg_{\mathbf a, \mathbf a', \delta} 1.
$$
The corollary follows on noting that
\[
\int_{\ker_G M}\prod_{i=1}^s f({\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(i)}, \tilde {\boldsymbol{{\gamma}}}^{(i)}) \mathrm{d} \mu_{\ker_G M} \geqslant (\delta/2)^s \mu_{\ker_G M} (\mathcal A^s\cap \ker_G M),
\]
and that $\ker_G M$ is isomorphic to $K(\mathbf a,d) \times K(\mathbf a', d')$.
